identity.name: Robert Jackson
identity.narrative: I drive for Uber and Lyft full-time. The robotaxis are my direct competition. Already seeing fewer rides.

historical_conditioning.lesson: Institutions can fail. Savings matter. Trust is fragile.
Remote work is possible. Government can provide. Disruption is sudden.

perception.sentiment: The denial broke. Not completely — Robert is not in free fall — but the specific combination of a company name, a city name, and a two-month timeline did something that generalized anxiety about automation could not do. It made the threat concrete. He is now operating in a different register: frightened but not frozen. The fear is functional, which is the best version of fear. He sat in a gas station parking lot for twelve minutes processing something he couldn't process while driving. He is not telling Marcus anything. He is holding the external presentation of stability very tightly. Underneath: a sustained high-stress hum, occasional intrusive calculations in the middle of the night, a specific new guilt about the brakes. He is a man who has spent six years being competent at one thing and is now staring at a horizon where that competence expires. He has not yet grieved that. He is not ready to. He is doing what he knows how to do — working — while trying, for the first time, to look sideways at what else might exist.

archetype: I used to think the hustle was enough. Show up, work hard, know your city, take care of your customers. That's always been my identity. I'm starting to see that the hustle is real — the work ethic is real — but I've been applying it to a shrinking market and calling that a strategy. That's not who I want to be. I want to be the guy who saw it coming and did something before he had no options left. I don't know if I'm that guy yet. But I'm trying to become him while there's still time. Two months is not a lot of time. It's also not zero time. I have to do something with it besides just drive.
